claims.text: An organisational structure is the levels of management and divisions of responsibilities within an organisation. It clarifies who performs each role, who may decide and who reports to whom. This can reduce duplicated work and gaps where everyone assumes someone else is responsible. In a centralised structure most decisions are retained at the centre or higher management levels. In a decentralised structure many decisions are delegated to lower levels. The distinction concerns the location of decision-making authority, not the number of buildings or whether the business uses computers. A structure can combine central financial policy with decentralised local service decisions. Clear roles help accountability, but the chart alone cannot ensure cooperation or competent decisions. Structure should fit the scale, activities and skills of the enterprise.

claims.text: Hierarchy arranges roles by authority; responsibility is the duty to complete work; authority is the right to make decisions and give instructions; span of control counts direct subordinates; chain of command traces the formal route from higher to lower levels; centralisation keeps most decisions near the top; delegation gives a subordinate authority for particular tasks while final responsibility remains with the delegating manager. These concepts describe different features of the same structure. In an organisation chart, use boxes for positions and lines for direct reporting relationships. A manager’s span counts the roles directly linked below that manager, not every person at lower levels. A long chain may support close supervision but delay messages; a wide span can reduce supervisory layers but may overburden a manager if tasks are complex. The effect depends on staff competence, work difficulty and support systems.

claims.text: The features of a structure interact. Adding supervisors can narrow a manager’s direct span and provide closer support, but it can also add a level to the chain of command. Removing levels may speed formal communication while widening the remaining managers’ spans. Delegation can relieve a bottleneck by authorising a subordinate to decide, but responsibility, resources and limits must be clear. A manager cannot meaningfully expect someone to resolve customer complaints while denying authority to offer any remedy. Central control can preserve consistency for high-risk or expensive decisions; local discretion can improve response where staff understand customers and have the necessary competence. Judge these effects in context because neither a tall nor a flat structure has a guaranteed performance advantage. An organisation chart shows the formal structure, not informal friendships or how well people cooperate.

claims.text: To draw a simple organisation chart, identify the most senior position, group positions at the correct levels and join each subordinate to the position it reports to directly. Use role titles rather than a list of names without jobs. Do not connect neighbouring roles merely because they are at the same level: a connecting line would imply a reporting relationship not stated. Keep direct spans distinguishable from all lower-level staff. The chart makes formal authority visible and helps a new worker identify a supervisor, but it does not show the quality of management or the informal communication network. Check the finished chart against each reporting fact. A line accidentally bypassing a supervisor changes the structure even if all job titles are present.

claims.text:
Omano Supplies has an owner-manager. Production, sales and finance heads each report to the owner-manager. claims.text: A small owner can coordinate a few staff directly, but growth may increase the number, variety and location of decisions beyond that person’s capacity. Appointing functional managers can introduce specialist skills and clarify responsibility. Delegating routine decisions can let local staff respond sooner and free senior management for wider planning. These changes require competent staff, clear authority and communication. More levels may lengthen the formal chain, increasing delay or distortion; extra managers also cost money. Alternatively, flattening the structure may shorten communication while giving remaining managers wider spans. Expansion does not dictate one correct shape. A business with risky technical work may need closer supervision than one with experienced staff carrying out familiar tasks. Review whether the proposed changes solve the actual overload and whether control remains adequate.

claims.text: Businesses can group work by function, product, market or systems. Functional organisation groups similar activities, such as finance and marketing. Product organisation groups responsibility around different products or product ranges. Market organisation groups work around customer markets, which may be geographical areas or customer types. Systems organisation can use project-based teams bringing different skills together to complete a defined piece of work. These approaches answer different coordination needs and can be combined. A product division may still contain functional specialists. Grouping by function does not, by itself, establish whether decisions are centralised: finance staff can be grouped together while some spending authority is delegated elsewhere. The organisation should make reporting and responsibility clear so that coordination across groups does not become a dispute about who decides.
